name: Lambton Worm

attributes.attribute: a dragon in the Norse and Saxon sense of the word worm
killed by spiky armor at the River Wear
home of the lords of Lambton

sources: Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
description: A lord hauls in a strange creature, a sort of Eel with nine mouths. He throws it down a Well—still locally called Worm’s Well—and sets about to reform his life. He even goes to the Crusades. Meanwhile, in the well, the worm is growing larger and larger, until it emerges a true monster to ravage the countryside and kill all the knights sent to combat it. When the lord returns from the Holy Land, he finds his lands in disarray and his people in fear.
text: The Lambton Worm is a famous figure in British folklore. The word worm can seem to name a small creature, but in Norse and Saxon speech it meant dragon. The story tells of a worm that haunted the land near Lambton Castle. It began with a lord in the fourteenth century who went fishing on a Sunday instead of going to church. As the church bells stopped, something took his line. He pledged to kill the worm. A wise woman told him to wear spiky armor and fight from the rock in the River Wear. She said he must slay the first being that met him on the journey home. Returning with the armor, he brought a hound to the gateway. The worm drove itself onto the spikes and perished, yet the lord sent the hound to death too late. From that fault, no lord of Lambton died quietly in his bed for nine generations.

okr.objective: Present the Lambton Worm as a dragon figure whose defeat carried a lasting curse.
key_results: Define worm as the Norse and Saxon word for dragon.
Describe the Sunday fishing lord and the wise woman's advice.
State that no lord of Lambton died in bed for nine generations.
